items.title: OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock
items.description: Developers increasingly use Codex with Amazon Bedrock to explore unfamiliar code, make changes, and handle repetitive engineering work. For platform teams, the challenge is to make those tools available without creating a second model-access, identity, and operations stack. Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. In this post, we show how to fit that path into the AWS identity, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Regional, and observability practices your organization already uses. Codex still runs on the developer workstation. The main design choice is how its model requests reach Amazon Bedrock and where your organization applies policy and operational controls. We begin with a small, least-privilege pilot and work through the checks that matter before access expands. The examples use GPT-5.6 Sol. Before starting the pilot, review Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock to confirm that Sol, Terra, or Luna is available in the AWS Region and inference path you plan to use. Recommended default: Start with Native AWS Access for a small, least-privilege pilot. Choose AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. A custom integration is the advanced version of the LLM Gateway pattern, not a quick start. The examples come from the open source Guidance for Codex on AWS repository. It includes quick starts for Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), and the Amazon CloudWatch setup used later in the post. Choose the quick start that matches your architecture, use it for the pilot, and adapt it to your environment. Choose your rollout path Authentication is only one part of an enterprise rollout. Decide who can use the service and which models and Regions are approved. Also define where configuration lives, what telemetry to collect, how usage is allocated, and which skills or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are allowed. The following table maps those needs to an access path and an owning team. Choose the access path that provides the controls you need now. The most straightforward path that meets the requirement usually has the lowest operational overhead. Decision rules Native AWS Access is the usual starting point when AWS identity and IAM controls are enough for the pilot. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Within the platform, AgentCore Gateway fits teams that want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, or related controls. A large language model (LLM) Gateway fits organizations that already operate a gateway or want to enforce controls in the request path. Building a custom gateway is the advanced version of this option. The following diagram compares where identity, routing, policy, telemetry, and operational ownership sit across the three rollout paths. Figure 1: Codex runs on the developer workstation in each scenario. Native AWS Access uses AWS IAM Identity Center, a configured AgentCore Gateway can apply managed routing and Guardrails, and a configured LLM Gateway can apply request-path controls Native AWS Access If Native AWS Access fits the pilot, the repository’s Native AWS Access quick start provides the complete procedure and supporting files. The following abbreviated walkthrough focuses on the sequence and the checks that matter most. Use your workforce identity provider for sign-in Employees continue to sign in through the identity provider they already use. In this example, Okta handles authentication through Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) and provisions users and groups into IAM Identity Center through System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM). IAM Identity Center then issues the temporary AWS credentials used by Codex. The identity provider is not configured in Codex. Prerequisites Add each pilot user to a dedicated group in the workforce identity system and provision that group to IAM Identity Center. Keep the assignment limited to the pilot. Choose an Amazon Bedrock Region and an OpenAI model available to the pilot identity, plus an inference profile if the selected API requires one. Check Sol, Terra, and Luna separately for the chosen account, Region, and inference path. Grant only the Amazon Bedrock model inference permissions used by Codex, any direct validation commands, and the selected observability destination. Prepare a non-production repository and name a rollback owner. Configure The pilot has three checks. First, sign in using the IAM Identity Center profile configured for the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and call Amazon Bedrock Runtime directly. Next, point Codex to the approved model. Finally, run a safe Codex task. The direct call isolates AWS access problems. The final step confirms the Codex configuration. Step 1: Sign in and validate Amazon Bedrock Runtime access. aws sso login --profile codex-bedrock export AWS_PROFILE=codex-bedrock aws bedrock-runtime converse --model-id us.openai.gpt-5.6-sol --messages '[{"role":"user","content":[{"text":"Reply with OK"}]}]' --region us-east-2 This command creates a short-lived AWS session and checks whether the profile can invoke the chosen model in the chosen Region. If it fails, resolve the profile, Region, model or inference-profile access, or IAM permissions before configuring Codex. Step 2: Configure the Codex provider. # ~/.codex/config.toml (or managed user configuration) model_provider = "amazon-bedrock" model = "openai.gpt-5.6-sol" [model_providers.amazon-bedrock.aws] profile = "codex-bedrock" region = "us-east-2" The model value is the Codex model ID. The profile selects the AWS IAM Identity Center session, and region tells Codex which AWS Region to use. Keep

items.title: Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification
items.description: When reviewing code, you start with a diff. You wouldn’t compare two 3,000-line files by eye and hope to spot every change. Formal policies can be even harder to compare because a textual diff often highlights syntactic changes that don’t affect meaning. Reorder two conjuncts, swap the arguments of an equality, or use an equivalent predicate, and much of the file might appear changed. A real change in behavior, such as an Or where the requirement says and , can get lost in that noise. A semantic diff shows what two policies have in common and where they disagree. The open source engine used in this post computes this diff using anti-unification , which finds a most specific common pattern for two expressions. Plotkin’s 1970 paper gives the classical formulation. The engine works over an e-graph, which keeps track of expressions known to be equal. We supply the algebraic laws and domain rules that justify those equalities, such as equating an external destination with one that isn’t internal. The result shows the shared parts once and keeps both versions of each differing part for review. If no differences remain, the policies are equivalent under those laws and rules. When the rules or the search are incomplete, a remaining difference might reflect an equivalence the engine has not found. One use case is autoformalization. Autoformalization translates natural language into a formal language. Suppose you want to turn requirements into SMT-LIB , the standard input language for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers such as Z3 and cvc5, or into Cedar or Dogwood to control authorization in your software system. A large language model (LLM) generates the formal artifact from the prose. The model writes the artifact. It plays no part in computing the diff. Run the model twice, and it might produce two different formalizations, with no ground truth to identify the correct one. A semantic diff shows where they agree and where they differ. Generate more candidates by varying the model, prompt, or sampling temperature. Comparing them shows which parts stay the same and which vary. Review the varying parts first. Requirements can also become OpenShell sandbox policies or Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions. OpenShell uses YAML to describe an agent’s filesystem and network access. CEL is embedded in applications to evaluate expressions, including policy conditions. These languages and formats differ in what they express, but translations into any of them can disagree about a condition, a scope, or an event. The following table gives illustrative disagreements: Language or format Policy focus Example disagreement Cedar Who can perform an action on a resource, under which conditions. One translation requires ownership and approval. Another accepts either. Dogwood Authorization involving the current request and recent event history. One translation checks a successful prior response. Another checks a request event. OpenShell policies An agent’s filesystem and network access, including rules for particular binaries. One translation permits repository-scoped GET . Another permits organization-scoped POST . CEL Conditions evaluated over inputs supplied by a host application. One translation requires production for both allowed ports. Another requires it for only one. In each worked example, we compare translations of the same requirement within one policy context. We encode the relevant syntax as terms and declare the equalities used in the comparison. The engine reads these encodings. It doesn’t import native policies from the four formats. The idea is a formal-methods analogue of semantic entropy , described by Farquhar et al. in Nature (2024). That approach samples several natural-language answers, clusters those that entail one another, and reports a single number. For formal outputs, anti-unification preserves more information. It identifies the shared structure and each divergence instead of returning only a score. Counterexamples help explain the consequences of a disagreement. An SMT solver can find a concrete assignment that satisfies one formula and violates the other. A reviewer can then trace that assignment through the formulas to understand the conflicting decisions. The anti-unifier gives a different view: it organizes the shared structure and the fragments that differ, without issuing an SMT query. A solver or policy validator can help resolve those fragments. We assume you can read S-expression syntax, as in SMT-LIB, and know what an authorization policy is. E-graphs and anti-unification are explained as they come up. When several translations agree on part of a requirement, the diff shows that part once. Where they disagree, it keeps the alternatives visible for review. How semantic diffing represents disagreement Say a policy-generation pipeline hands you two candidate rules for this requirement: sensitive data sent to an external destination must be encrypted . Rule A Rule B sensitive ( data ) ∧ external ( dst ) → encrypted ¬ internal ( dst ) ∧ sensitive ( data ) → audited Whether these are the same rule isn’t obvious. The conditions are reordered, external is expressed indirectly as not internal , and the conclusions do not match. The engine computes a most specific anti-unifier for these terms. In its input language, the two rules are S-expressions. items.title: Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
items.description: Silent data corruption (SDC) happens when hardware, such as a GPU, returns a wrong but plausible number and raises no error. In distributed training, the wrong number can flow into the gradients and weights of every replica. Loss can still look normal for hours, and by the time a team notices an unexplained divergence or a weaker model, the compute is spent. It happens at scale: during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on up to 16K H100 GPUs, Meta attributed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions to silent data corruption, and those were only the cases that interrupted the job and were traced to SDC. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod already replaces nodes that report a fault: the health-monitoring agent watches for GPU errors, deep health checks stress-test nodes, and automatic node recovery swaps out bad hardware. SDC slips past all of these features, because the hardware never reports anything. Detection has to come from the training job itself. In this post, we add three checks to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop to detect SDC. When a check fires, we map the suspect rank to its node, contain the corruption, and have SageMaker HyperPod replace the node. Each check covers a different place where a fault can land: A non-finite gradient check catches NaN, Inf, and overflow in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step it happens, and NaN or Inf that the gradient all-reduce introduces. A ring replay audit catches finite wrong values. On audit steps, every GPU recomputes a micro-batch from another node and compares the loss bit for bit and the gradients by fingerprint. A weight fingerprint comparison catches corruption in the optimizer step and in stored weights, by comparing every replica’s weights after the update. We tested the checks with software-injected faults on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs), and repeated every test on three instances, the minimum the checks need. The full code of this solution is available in the accompanying GitHub repository . How silent data corruption happens and why the usual checks miss it SDC comes from manufacturing defects (marginal transistors that slip past vendor screening) and silicon aging in a specific compute unit, most often a multiply-accumulate lane in a tensor core, which is exactly the hardware model training hammers. That marginal circuit computes correctly most of the time and wrong only under stress: high temperature, voltage droop, or specific operand patterns. Because the arithmetic logic path has no ECC or parity (unlike memory), the wrong result, say 4.0001 instead of 4.0000, is never flagged, and it flows through activations and gradients into every replica’s weights. The reason it is so hard to catch is that SDC is in the compute path, and every integrity check you already have guards a different boundary : Check What it guards Why it misses SDC ECC memory Catches bit flips in memory, not wrong math. There is no ECC on a tensor-core result. Xid errors (NVRM) GPU driver/hardware faults The GPU raises an Xid when it detects a fault. SDC by definition raises none, so nothing lands in /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/ HMA logs. DCGM deep health check hardware faults Misses defects that need your workload’s operands, thermal state, or timing. Runs on an idle node, outside your job. NVLink / PCIe / EFA checksums transport Verify bytes arrived as sent, not that they were computed correctly. Checkpoint checksums storage round-trip A poisoned-but-consistent checkpoint checksums fine. The way to catch SDC is to check the result of the computation itself. Solution overview The loop has four steps. Your training job does the first two, and the last two use Kubernetes and SageMaker HyperPod features: Step 1. Detect: Three checks in your training loop name a suspect GPU by comparing data-parallel replicas. Step 2. Localize: On SageMaker HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), the Kubernetes node name contains the instance ID, so mapping a suspect rank to a node is a lookup. Step 3. Contain and correlate: Stop the job, cordon the node, and look at its GPU metrics in the SageMaker HyperPod observability dashboards. Step 4. Confirm and recover: Confirm when the alarm is ambiguous, replace the node after review, and resume from a checkpoint saved before the suspect window. Figure 1: A SageMaker HyperPod EKS cluster with three p5 nodes running training pods and SDC checks. Node 1 raises an alarm for rank 13, and the proposed steps cordon the node, check GPU metrics, replace it, and restart training It helps to see the loop as layers, each adding something different: Layer Source What it adds Catches truly silent SDC? 1. Non-finite gradient check Your training script Names a GPU whose local gradient is NaN or Inf, before the all-reduce, and stops the step if the reduced gradient is NaN or Inf Only faults that become NaN, Inf, or overflow 2. Ring replay audit Your training script Every GPU recomputes another node’s micro-batch and compares the loss bits and gradient fingerprints Yes, for finite compute-path faults that change the loss or a gradient, on audit steps 3. Weight fingerprint comparison Your training script Names a replica whose weights differ from a strict majority after the update Yes, for optimizer-step and stored-weight faults on one copy. Blind to compute-path faults and to sharded weights 4. Localization Your training script, using SageMaker HyperPod node names Maps a suspect rank to an instance ID from the Kubernetes node name n/a: it localizes 5. DCGM correlation HyperPod observability add-on The suspect GPU’s DCGM metrics around the alarm It confirms faults only where they also appear in hardware counters. Clean telemetry doesn’t clear a node. 6. Deep health check StartClusterHealthCheck (DCGM L4) An on-demand hardware diagnostic on the suspect node It catches hardware defects its own test patterns trigger. Triage, not proof 7

items.title: Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: AI agents and applications that answer questions about recent events, product releases, prices, or regulations need information newer than their model’s training data. Until now, Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore delivered that information to agents through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. That means creating a gateway and a web search target and calling the tool from an MCP client. The setup fits platform teams that share one search policy across many agents, but it’s more than you need when your own code only requires search results. Today, we’re announcing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With it, your own code can search the web with a single API call. It returns ranked results from a web index that Amazon operates, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. You call it from the AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), signed with the same AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials you use for your other AWS services. There are no resources to create first. Authenticate, call, and get results. Use it in an application, an agent loop you write yourself, or a data pipeline. Why a standalone API? The AgentCore Gateway is the recommended path for most agentic workloads. It gives agents one secure Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that combines web search with your other tools. It also handles inbound and outbound authentication, semantic tool selection, and optional MCP sessions . But developers told us they also need a lower-level integration point for scenarios where the gateway is not the right fit: Custom orchestration frameworks – Developers building their own agent loops, or using frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex, want to call web search directly as a tool within their orchestration logic rather than routing through a gateway. Non-agent use cases – Not every application that needs web grounding is an agent. Search-powered dashboards, fact-checking pipelines, content enrichment workflows, and monitoring systems all benefit from real-time web results without requiring agent infrastructure. Tighter control over the request lifecycle – Some developers want to manage retries, caching, and error handling themselves rather than delegating to the gateway. Simpler integration for existing applications – Applications that already have their own API layer can call the Web Search API directly, adding web grounding without adopting the full AgentCore Gateway stack. The Web Search API complements the gateway. It runs on the same search infrastructure that powers Alexa+, Kiro, Quick, and other Amazon products, with the same quality and compliance posture, exposed as a direct API operation. How it works The Web Search API is the InvokeWebSearch operation on the bedrock-agentcore data plane, the same endpoint that other AgentCore tools such as AgentCore Browser , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, use. Requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) from your standard AWS credentials, so there’s no API key or secret to manage. Figure 1: How a Web Search API request flows The numbered steps are: Your application calls InvokeWebSearch with the AWS SDKs or the AWS CLI, which sign the request with SigV4 using its AWS credentials. From a virtual private cloud (VPC), the call can go through an interface VPC endpoint. The API checks with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) that the caller has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch on the AWS managed web search tool. The API applies the filters in the request: the domains to include or exclude and the publication time range. The API searches a web index that Amazon operates. Queries are served inside AWS and aren’t sent to a third-party search engine. The API returns up to maxResults ranked results, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. The calling identity needs one IAM permission on an AWS managed resource. It’s the same action and resource that a gateway’s service role uses for web search, so one policy covers both routes. For details, see Grant permission to call the API . { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "InvokeWebSearch", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch", "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:aws:tool/web-search.v1" } ] } A first search request The following example searches two trusted domains for pages published in 2026, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) : import boto3 client = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore", region_name="us-west-2") response = client.invoke_web_search( webSearchId="web-search.v1", searchQuery="multi-region EKS cluster deployment best practices", maxResults=10, filters={ "domainFilter": {"include": ["aws.amazon.com", "kubernetes.io"]}, "publishedDateFilter": {"publishedAfter": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}, }, ) for result in response["results"]: print(result.get("publishedAt"), result.get("title"), result.get("url")) Every result has a text extract. The title, URL, and publication date come back when the index has them, so read them with get . One result from a live call, shortened: { "title": "One Amazon EKS, many edges: How to choose your edge container strategy on AWS", "url": "https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/one-amazon-eks-many-edges-how-to-choose-your-edge-container-strategy-on-aws/", "text": "Separate the standard from the deployment model Choosing the wrong platform isn't really the issue. ...", "publishedAt": "2026-09-25T15:52:00Z" } That’s the full integration. If your code runs on AWS Lambda , Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) , Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) , or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) , the execution role provides credentials automatically. Add the permission to that role, and the same code runs unchanged. Key API features Domain filtering – Include or exclude specific do

items.title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026
items.description: At AWS, we believe AI builders should be able to choose the right model for every task, trust their agents in production, and see clearly what their AI workloads cost. That belief guides how we invest across our portfolio. Amazon Bedrock gives you access to leading models and the tools to build and scale AI applications securely. We extend this foundation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , which provides the platform to build, connect, and optimize agents using any model and any framework. That includes Strands , our open source agent development toolkit. Together, they take you from first prototype to production. As agents move into core business workflows, the bar rises. You need the flexibility to use different models as tasks, budgets, and latency targets change. When a primary model is throttled or unreachable, your agents must keep working. They also must act within limits you set and return output other software can use as is. Their answers must stay grounded in sources you allow, and their cost must hold up at high volume. What we shipped in October addresses each of these needs. New models help you match each task to the right price and speed, from high-volume subagents to real-time voice. Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore updates keep agents available, hold them to the processes you define, and help you trust what they return. New pricing and cost reporting make spend more predictable. Strands adds new ways to build, contain, and test agents. Match the model to the task on Amazon Bedrock Run fast, low-cost subagents. Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for subagents and high-volume, cost-sensitive work. According to Anthropic, it is the most capable Haiku yet and costs around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. It is also the first Haiku with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence for each task. In a multi-agent setup, a model such as Claude Opus 5.5 can plan the work and hand well-defined coding, tool use, and browser automation tasks to Haiku. This keeps running many agents in parallel affordable. Get near-flagship results at a lower price. OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock. On OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation, it performed on par with GPT-6 Astra and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Its input and output token prices are at least 50 percent lower than those of GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It accepts text and images with up to 1 million input tokens, which suits drafting proposals, interpreting technical drawings, and building agents that work across business systems. For latency-sensitive work such as real-time coding assistants, GPT-6.1 Sol now also offers Ultrafast mode . Build voice agents that reason in real time. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic , our latest speech-to-speech model, improves reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling accuracy, with lower latency at the same price as Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. A customer service agent can now look up an order, check return eligibility, and start a return in a single conversation. Pick specialized models for coding and video. GLM 5.3 by Z.ai is an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon software engineering, with a 1-million-token context window and prompt caching, available to eligible enterprise customers. TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 turns entire videos into structured, time-coded metadata. It reads visuals, audio, and on-screen text in a single pass, with no separate ingestion pipeline. Use more models in AWS GovCloud (US). Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-5.6 models with cross-Region inference are now available in AWS GovCloud (US). Daybreak Red from OpenAI , a model for authorized security work, is available to eligible customers in AWS GovCloud (US-East). Regulated teams get more models while maintaining US data sovereignty. Build and run agents you can rely on Build and operate agents from your terminal. AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is now generally available in version 1.0 . We rebuilt it with faster startup, a consistent command structure, and support for more AgentCore resources. You can work with harnesses, runtimes, memory, identity, gateways, and payments directly or through a project. Existing projects move to version 1 with one command. The result is one tool from local development to day-to-day operations. Keep agents available when a model is throttled. AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now supports the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel APIs and model fallback . Your existing Amazon Bedrock SDK code can point at the gateway without per-provider code changes. When the primary model is throttled or unreachable, the gateway routes the request to the next model or provider in a chain you define. A circuit breaker skips destinations that are failing. The gateway can also reach private targets in your virtual private cloud (VPC) using certificates from your own private certificate authority . Your agents stay available without retry logic in every client. Turn your business workflows into agent tools. You can now use AWS Step Functions workflows , including your existing Standard and Express workflows, as tools through AgentCore Gateway. Your business logic stays in a workflow you already run and trust, so you don’t rebuild it inside the agent or rely on a prompt to follow it. The agent decides when to run a workflow, and Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. For example, a support agent can start your refund workflow, and every refund still goes through the same eligibility check, approval, and credit steps. Get JSON your systems can use as is. Structured outputs are now available for all Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. You receive schema-compliant JSON without custom parsing or retries. You can extract every required field from an earnings report, or route support tickets with entities that always match your data model. Keep answers grounded

items.title: Gemini Decisions API
items.description: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } } Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , gemini , llm-release , jev , decision-models

items.title: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track
items.description: From November 30th to December 4th, Amazon Web Services (AWS) will hold its annual premier learning event: re:Invent . At this event, attendees will become stronger and more proficient in various areas of AWS technology through a variety of experiences: keynotes given by AWS leaders, interactive working sessions led by AWS experts, and fun, immersive activities such as live entertainment and games at re:Play . There are over 2,000 learning sessions that focus on specific topics at various skill levels, and the AI/ML (AIM) track has more than 140 unique sessions for you to choose from. We’re here to help you identify the sessions that best fit your needs. Even if you can’t join in person, you can catch up with many of the sessions on demand and even watch the keynotes live. The basics: Session types If you can join us, then remember that we offer several types of sessions that can help maximize your learning in a variety of AWS topics. re:Invent attendees can choose to attend breakouts, chalk talks, builder sessions, workshops, and code talks. The breakout sessions are recorded and uploaded a few days after to the AWS Events YouTube channel , while the rest are live non-recorded interactive sessions. Here are the details for each session type: Breakout sessions: Attendees are in a lecture-style 60-minute informative session presented by AWS experts, customers, and partners. Chalk-talk sessions: Attendees interact with presenters, asking questions, and using a whiteboard in session. Builder sessions: Attendees participate in a one-hour session and build something. Workshop sessions: Attendees join a two-hour interactive session where you work in a small team to solve a real problem using AWS services. Code talk sessions: Attendees participate in engaging code-focused sessions where an expert leads a live coding session. Lightning talk sessions: Attendees watch a 20-minute demo dedicated to either a specific service or customer story (located in the Venetian Expo Hall or Wynn/Encore Upper Convention Promenade). With so many sessions to pick from, it helps to know how the pieces fit together. Here is how AWS thinks about its AI offerings, so you can decide where to begin and where to focus. The AWS AI stack overview and tie-in to re:Invent sessions AWS offers a comprehensive AI portfolio in the cloud. It covers everything from the physical infrastructure and AI chips that power AI workloads up through ready-to-use agentic solutions that teams can adopt today. Understanding how these services work together helps you navigate re:Invent and focus on the sessions most relevant to what you’re building. Figure 1: The AWS AI stack Global Infrastructure – It all starts with data centers designed and optimized for AI workloads. These facilities are built to handle the power, cooling, and networking demands that large AI training and inference jobs require. AI Chips – Running inside those data centers are two compute options: AWS Trainium , purpose-built for high-performance AI training and inference, and NVIDIA GPUs for teams that need GPU-based acceleration. Customers choose based on their workload, performance requirements, and cost targets. Data Foundation – AI is only as good as the data behind it. AWS Context connects your data across storage, databases, analytics, and search services, giving models and agents access to the right information at the right time. Models, Training, and Inferencing – This is where models get built, trained, fine-tuned, and served. Amazon Bedrock gives you managed access to hundreds of leading models from multiple providers through a unified API. Amazon SageMaker AI gives you full control to train, fine-tune, and deploy custom models on dedicated infrastructure. Many customers use both depending on the workload. Agent Development and Management – Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is where you build, deploy, and manage AI agents. It supports any model or provider mix, including models from both Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, so teams can design agents that pick the right model for each task without being locked into a single provider. Agentic Solutions – At the top of the stack sit purpose-built agents that are ready to use. Kiro helps developers ship correctly the first time with spec-driven development. AWS Quick connects your applications, tools, and data into a personal knowledge graph that learns how you work. Amazon Connect delivers agents for customer experience, hiring, supply chain, and healthcare. AWS Marketplace gives you access to partner-built AI solutions. Security, Governance, and Cost Optimization run across every layer of the AI stack. They are built into the foundation, with hardware-level isolation at the chip layer and controls that enforce what agents can access and do. The AI-focused sessions at re:Invent span the full stack. Whether you’re evaluating AI chips, serving models in production, building custom models, deploying agents, or adopting ready-to-use solutions, this guide helps you find the sessions that matter most. Use it to build a smarter re:Invent schedule. The artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) track primarily focuses on three core layers of this stack: AI chips , models, training, and inference , and agent development and management , with security, governance, and cost optimization woven throughout. The following sections start at the chip layer and move up through models and agents. Then come sessions that tie the stack together. The guide ends with other relevant topics, such as sustainability and infrastructure where you run your AI workloads. Within each section, sessions for newcomers come first and technical deep dives come last. Want to skip ahead? Jump straight to the topic you care about: AWS AI platform sessions AI chips: NVIDIA GPUs and AWS Trainium Amazon SageMaker AI sessions Build and run AI applications and agents with Amazon Bedrock Build AI that works with documents, voice, and images Building trust in AI

items.title: Automating AWS Agent Registry updates with push-based architecture
items.description: Every time a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server published in the AWS Agent Registry, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, gains a new tool or updates its schema, the registry record must be updated too. Without automated push-based sync, consumers discover stale metadata. For organizations managing multiple MCP servers across accounts, such a sync keeps catalog records current within an existing governance workflow. In most enterprise deployments, a catalog’s value depends on its freshness. If a developer deploys a new tool on Monday, but the registry record still reflects last week’s schema, consumers lose trust in the catalog. Stale metadata directly reduces registry reliability, leading teams to inadvertently build dependencies on inaccurate information. When an engineer adds a tool to an MCP server but forgets to update the catalog: Consumers miss out on the new capability entirely. Applications might call the tool using an outdated schema, causing unexpected runtime behavior or silent workflow deviations. Multiplied across teams, this lack of automation erodes trust in the registry. Organizations ultimately fall back on ad hoc discovery mechanisms like hardcoded endpoints, informal knowledge sharing, and stale documentation. In this post, we outline an event-driven architecture that automates these updates using AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Lambda. Architecture overview The following solution brings these services together into an event-driven pipeline that detects runtime changes and synchronizes them to the registry automatically. The architecture supports both multi-account and single-account environments: Single-account setup: For straightforward deployments, all components reside within Account A. Cross-account forwarding setup isn’t needed as events flow directly within Account A. Multi-account setup: This involves two accounts where runtime events from Account B are securely forwarded to Account A. Account A (registry account) owns the AWS Agent Registry, the Amazon EventBridge rule, the push-sync Lambda function, and CloudTrail logs. Account B (MCP server account) hosts the MCP server runtime and the Amazon Cognito OAuth provider used for authentication. The sample uses two accounts, but you can scale the architecture for multiple accounts, with Account A as the registry account and multiple AWS accounts similar to Account B for different MCP servers. The following diagram shows the end-to-end event flow for an update to an MCP server in Account B. The captured event is forwarded to Account A, where a Lambda function queries the MCP server for its tools and updates the matching registry record. Figure 1: End-to-end event flow for a cross-account MCP server update, from the CloudTrail event in Account B to the registry record update in Account A. The architecture uses five AWS services: AWS CloudTrail captures UpdateAgentRuntime API calls as management events. Amazon EventBridge routes matching events to the Lambda function, with cross-account forwarding supported. AWS Lambda queries the MCP server for its current tools, diffs against the registry, and updates the record if changed. AWS Agent Registry stores MCP server records and their tool schemas as the central source of truth. AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, brokers OAuth token exchanges securely, so the Lambda authenticates without storing secrets. How it works: business logic flow After it’s deployed, the pipeline runs the following end-to-end workflow: Trigger : A developer in Account B updates an MCP server, which calls the UpdateAgentRuntime API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS CloudTrail captures the event. Route : Amazon EventBridge catches the CloudTrail event and forwards it to the central event bus in Account A . Parse : The sync Lambda in Account A extracts the runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) from the event payload and dynamically constructs the MCP server’s invocation URL. This is how it knows which server in Account B to query. Authenticate : The Lambda generates a secure OAuth bearer token through AgentCore Identity. Fetch : The Lambda calls the MCP server ( initialize , then tools/list ) to retrieve the latest tools information. Sync : The Lambda finds the matching registry record by its ARN, evaluates the differences, and updates the registry if the schema has changed. This flow assumes that the Agent Registry in Account A already contains a pre-registered record for the MCP server (created during initial onboarding). The Lambda function in this sample updates existing records only. It doesn’t generate new ones. This same flow works in a single-account setup where all resources (registry, Lambda, Amazon EventBridge rule, and MCP server) reside in one account. In that case, skip the cross-account forwarding step. Events flow directly within the same account’s Amazon EventBridge bus. Technical walkthrough This section walks through the workflow for a single MCP server update with two accounts as depicted in the architecture diagram. The same flow executes independently for each server that emits an UpdateAgentRuntime event. The Lambda handles one event at a time, scaling naturally with the Amazon EventBridge invocation model. Step 1: Event capture and routing for cross-account setup When a developer deploys or updates an MCP server, the UpdateAgentRuntime API is called, either by the AgentCore CLI ( agentcore deploy ) or directly. AWS CloudTrail records this as a management event in Account B, with a delivery delay of approximately 5–15 minutes. The event is then delivered to Account A’s default Amazon EventBridge bus. For a cross-account setup, Account B’s Amazon EventBridge forwards matching events to Account A’s event bus through a cross-account rule. items.title: How DXC Technology built a multi-model AI substrate on Amazon Bedrock
items.description: This post is co-written with Nick Tamburro of DXC Technology. When an AI agent can act on a production server at a bank or a hospital, access to a capable foundation model is only the starting point. Recent public incidents, in which autonomous agents took destructive actions their operators never intended, show that the real risk is rarely the model alone. It’s an agent holding more authority than its task requires, with nothing in the architecture to stop it. Avoiding that starts with a substrate that governs model access at the infrastructure level. Amazon Bedrock provides that substrate. Through a single managed interface, it gives DXC OASIS access to multiple foundation models: Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova , Meta Llama, and open-weight families. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforce content filtering, personally identifiable information (PII) redaction, and denied-topic policies uniformly across every model. AWS PrivateLink keeps inference traffic within the customer’s virtual private cloud (VPC), and serverless scaling avoids self-managed GPU infrastructure as a failure point. Because these are system-level controls rather than bolt-ons, they gave DXC Technology a governed foundation for what no model layer can deliver on its own: a trusted harness that orchestrates, governs, and audits AI agents across enterprise IT operations at scale. Model availability varies by AWS Region. See Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . DXC Technology runs managed IT services for some of the world’s most regulated organizations: banks, hospitals, and government agencies. With more than 115,000 employees across 70 countries, DXC operates mission-critical systems where resilience and governance are non-negotiable. When DXC set out to build DXC OASIS, the harness for mission-critical IT operations, the team separated the problem into two layers. The first is a governed model substrate built on Amazon Bedrock. The second is the trusted harness built on top: DXC’s own orchestration, governance, and assurance layer. In this post, we explore how DXC built the resilient, flexible model substrate beneath DXC OASIS on Amazon Bedrock. We also show where DXC drew the line between what the substrate provides and what the harness must provide. Since general availability in March 2026, DXC OASIS has reduced resolution time by 95% on average across 56 measured use cases. Across every model, customer data stays within the AWS data boundary: prompts and completions are not shared with third-party model providers and are not used to train the underlying foundation models. “Our customers operate complex, business-critical environments and need both choice and resilience in how they adopt AI. Amazon Bedrock provides access to a broad ecosystem of models with the governance, security, and operational controls required at enterprise scale. That flexibility allows us to use the right model for the right task, adapt as technology evolves, and stay focused on delivering measurable business outcomes for our customers.” — Dan Gray, President, GIS, DXC Technology Solution overview DXC OASIS separates the question of which model from the question of how work gets done. Amazon Bedrock is the substrate: a governed gateway to foundation models (FMs), reachable through one consistent API, with security and networking controls that keep traffic inside the AWS perimeter. The harness is everything DXC builds on top: orchestration across tools and systems, operational context drawn from 60 years of runbooks and escalation logic, policy enforcement, human-oversight gates, and full auditability of every agent action. The design goals were: Resilience: No single point of failure at the model layer. Flexibility: Route each task to the most appropriate model on cost, latency, and capability. Regulatory sovereignty: Meet the data-handling expectations of regulated tenants. Safety by design: Bound what every agent can do, so that no action with operational impact runs without policy checks and, where required, human approval. The main risk DXC designed against was coupling the system to any single provider, framework, or deployment target. The following diagram shows the key AWS services in the DXC DXC OASIS architecture. Engineers and operators reach the system through Amazon Route 53 and an Application Load Balancer inside the customer’s Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) . The DXC OASIS agent runtime runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) in a private subnet. There, a supervisor agent delegates to capability agents that draw on a knowledge base, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) . Every model call leaves the subnet through a VPC interface endpoint and AWS PrivateLink to reach Amazon Bedrock, so inference traffic doesn’t traverse the public internet. AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) , AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , TLS 1.2, Amazon CloudWatch, VPC Flow Logs, AWS CloudTrail, and OpenTelemetry provide security and observability across every layer. Figure 1: The DXC OASIS architecture on AWS Building the DXC OASIS substrate DXC began building DXC OASIS as a prototype in early 2025. A cross-functional team reached general availability in March 2026, scaling toward 130 customer environments on Amazon EKS with per-tenant namespaces and GitOps rollout. items.title: Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets
items.description: If you’re building generative AI solutions, reusable assets can help you stop rebuilding components that already exist: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, document processors, agent scaffolding, and so on. This has a compounding cost: time not spent solving the customer’s actual problem. This post shows you how to access a curated catalog of 23 production-ready assets from the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, now part of AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services. These assets can reduce your development time from months to weeks, with evidence from companies like DoorDash , Lyft , and Ricoh . Since 2023, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center has published open source reusable assets. These production-grade building blocks give you a validated foundation to start from instead of a blank file. These assets have powered customer solutions delivering measurable results: 50x increases in testing capacity, 90 percent reductions in engineering hours, and deployment timelines compressed from months to weeks. In this post, you will learn why teams keep rebuilding generative AI components, what makes an asset truly reusable, how companies like DoorDash and Ricoh achieved measurable results by using these assets, and how to access and deploy 23 open source assets from the catalog. For a complete list of all available assets, see the asset catalog at the end of this post. The problem: Why teams keep rebuilding Three root causes drive redundant development across generative AI teams: No single source of truth – Assets scatter across repositories, wikis, and drives. Builders can’t find what exists, so they rebuild from scratch. No quality signal – Without verification of production readiness, security reviews, or maintenance status, builders have no way to trust existing solutions and default to writing their own code. No reuse culture – Sharing remains informal and ungoverned. What one team builds stays with that team, and problems get solved repeatedly. The cost of rebuilding compounds. Each redundant build consumes engineering hours, delays customer delivery, and creates maintenance burden. Even AI-generated code requires production hardening, security reviews, testing at scale, and ongoing maintenance. These assets arrive already validated, security-reviewed, and production-grade, avoiding that verification burden. When teams finally reach production, they’ve spent weeks on undifferentiated heavy lifting, work that should have been reusable from day one. The AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services resolves this challenge through reusable assets. What a reusable asset actually is A reusable asset isn’t a code snippet or a sample. It’s a production-grade, composable building block that implements a discrete generative AI capability. Reusable assets are validated for quality and security before publication. They include clear deployment guides for discoverability and are instrumented to track adoption across customer engagements. These assets are maintained across their lifecycle. Examples from the catalog include RAG pipeline components, document ingestion modules, agent scaffolding templates, evaluation frameworks, and prompt management patterns. The assets are tested in production environments, reviewed for security compliance, and refined based on real customer feedback. This is the difference between a one-off artifact and a building block you can trust. Real results: Customer success stories The value of reusable assets isn’t theoretical. Here’s what happens when teams build on proven foundations instead of starting from scratch. Contact Center GenAI Agent: DoorDash and Lyft According to the AWS case study, DoorDash built a fully voice-operated self-service generative AI contact center solution using the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset. As reported, the solution handles over 100,000 calls per day with 2.5-second response latency, achieving a 50x increase in testing capacity. Using Amazon Bedrock reduced development time by 50 percent. The team reached live testing readiness in 2 months. Lyft used the same Contact Center GenAI Agent asset to bring agentic AI to life for riders and drivers, demonstrating the asset’s versatility across different customer engagement models. The Contact Center GenAI Agent provides automated question answering capabilities for both text and voice channels. It employs a RAG architecture to facilitate multi-turn conversations while maintaining context. The solution integrates with Amazon Connect and uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , a fully managed RAG capability, for hybrid search and metadata filtering. Learn more: DoorDash Case Study Lyft Case Study Contact Center GenAI agent blog post GenAI Intelligent Document Processing: Ricoh Ricoh serves major health insurance payers, managed care organizations, and healthcare providers. These customers process hundreds of thousands of critical documents each month, including insurance claims, grievances, appeals, and clinical records. As Ricoh scaled to serve more healthcare customers, they needed a standardized, multi-tenant document processing approach. That approach had to onboard new implementations without requiring unique development and tuning for each one. Using the Accelerated Intelligent Document Processing on AWS asset as a foundation, Ricoh built a standardized, multi-tenant solution for automated document classification and extraction. This transformed their document processing from a custom-engineering bottleneck into a scalable, repeatable service. Results: As documented in the published case study, Ricoh achieved a 7-fold throughput increase, from 10,000–70,000 documents monthly. Engineering hours per deployment dropped by over 90 percent (80 hours to under 5). Onboarding time fell from 4–6 weeks to 2–3 days. items.title: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
items.description: The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game. This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance "declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity." Noting "a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools," the group of jurors called out AI's ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still "not a foregone conclusion in our industry." items.title: Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick
items.description: This blog post focuses on how AI can improve and expedite the product development life cycle using agents built on AWS Quick, with human approval baked into the process. AI-driven software delivery is helping teams ship products faster than ever. As implementation accelerates, the upstream product development process becomes even more important. Coding agents can turn clear requirements into working software faster than before, but they can’t compensate for building the wrong product. With implementation becoming easier, your competitive advantage moves upstream to four critical activities: discovering the right customer problem, deciding which opportunity to pursue, designing the right experience, and validating it through a prototype. The signals that you need to make those decisions are scattered everywhere. Your customers leave feedback in Slack, your sales team logs insights in Salesforce, systems record incidents in ServiceNow, stakeholders document requirements in Microsoft SharePoint, engineers track work items in Jira, and teams make decisions in Outlook meetings and email threads. As your teams move between these tools, they disconnect context from the decisions it should inform, and lose more at every handoff. AWS Quick provides the connective layer for this fragmented knowledge. By grounding custom chat agents in connected enterprise data and storing their artifacts in shared Spaces , AWS Quick helps your team build with existing organizational knowledge instead of starting each initiative from a blank page. The AI-Driven Product Development Lifecycle (AI-PDLC) is a framework that applies these capabilities through a suite of six AWS Quick agents with specialized skills, producing a traceable set of artifacts at each phase. Agents gather and structure context, surface gaps, and draft artifacts. You and your team contribute judgment and approve every decision. The objective isn’t to produce documents faster. It’s to help your team think better, preserve why each decision was made, and give engineering and coding agents a specification grounded in customer evidence. We will show you how to configure the six-agent AI-PDLC suite in AWS Quick and use it to move from distributed customer signals to a validated prototype. Throughout, it preserves context from the first insight through the engineering handoff. Architecture The diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the AI-PDLC framework. Figure 1: End-to-end AI-PDLC flow, from scattered enterprise signals through AWS Quick agents to the coding-agent handoff It starts with the signals most teams lose track of, that is, the Slack threads, Jira tickets, docs, and call transcripts that hold the why behind a decision and what customers actually said. Enterprise connectors pull that context from Slack, Outlook, Jira, Salesforce, SharePoint, ServiceNow, and many more enterprise sources. Figure 2: AWS Quick builds a personal knowledge graph that links people, projects, and decisions across connected apps and folders AWS Quick can build a personal knowledge graph from your connected apps and folders, linking the people, projects, and decisions across your tools. Those signals feed the brain: the set of agents on AWS Quick, led by an Orchestrator that runs Discovery, Prioritize, Working Backwards, Spec Generator, and Designer. Everything they produce lands in one common language: a prototype_spec.md holding the acceptance criteria, personas, screens, data model. Every decision traces back to a source. AWS Quick can delegate development tasks to AI coding agents using the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) . ACP is an open JSON-RPC 2.0 standard with no vendor lock-in. Customers can use their preferred coding agent like Kiro or Claude Code to build against the specification generated by AI-PDLC. Underneath it all runs a human approval gate at every stage. You validate the pain points, approve priorities, sign off the spec, gate the build, and accept the review. Production data then flows back into Discovery, closing the loop. The agents do the work while you make the calls, and nobody has to leave their tool to do it. Solution overview The AI-PDLC lifecycle spans eight phases: Discover, Decide, Design, Prototype, Engineer, Ship, Operate, and Learn. This post focuses on the first four, where the product team works. The last four are handled by coding agents such as Kiro, which build from the specifications the upstream phases produce. The upstream phases are implemented as six agents in AWS Quick. Figure 3: The upstream AI-PDLC phases implemented as six agents in AWS Quick Users interact only with an Orchestrator, which reads each specialist’s question framework at runtime, asks targeted questions for the current phase, and dispatches artifact generation to the right specialist. A single conversation drives the whole journey, and the pipeline advances only after human approval at each step in the workflow. Figure 4: A single Orchestrator conversation drives the pipeline, advancing only after human approval at each gate Phase 1: Discover The Discovery agent guides structured pain point analysis across interactive Q&A, URL ingestion, and direct pulls from connected enterprise sources like Slack, Jira, support tickets, Salesforce, and research repositories. It scores every pain point for severity and frequency, producing a Pain Point Board that gives the team one evidence-grounded view of what customers struggle with. Figure 5: The Discovery agent produces a Pain Point Board scored by severity and frequency Phase 2: Decide The Prioritize agent scores each use case against weighted criteria using two transparent 0–10 frameworks: one purpose-built for agentic use cases (large language model (LLM) capability match, tool availability, user acceptance) and one for traditional applications (feasibility, business impact, effort). items.title: UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents
items.description: Teams building AI agents on AWS use a range of frameworks, including LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each framework records agent execution in its own way, so the structure of messages, tool calls, and handoffs between agents differs from one to the next. Evaluation tooling tends to follow the same boundaries: teams build metrics, scoring logic, and result storage against a single framework’s trace format, and they must rebuild them when they switch frameworks or run agents on more than one. This coupling makes a basic development question harder to answer: did a change to the prompt, model, or tools improve the agent? Answering it requires consistent metrics across versions of an agent and a shared record of past results to compare against. Agent quality also spans several dimensions that a single accuracy score does not capture: tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi-turn conversation, multi-agent coordination, and reasoning. In this post, we introduce the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF). Customers across 12 organizations in the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries used UAEF to evaluate their AI agents with one consistent set of metrics and compare agent versions before release. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system: it uses adapters to convert traces from each framework into a common format, then scores those traces with 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions. It stores the results in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and generates reports and insights that inform the next iteration of the agent. This post describes how UAEF works, provides a playbook for choosing metrics and preparing datasets, and points to runnable notebooks for each supported framework. UAEF: One evaluation layer for agent frameworks UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system for AI agents. It takes the agent a team already has and scores it the same way across supported frameworks and runtimes. UAEF takes two inputs: the agent under test and a dataset to run it on. The dataset provides the inputs for each test case, and it can also include ground-truth answers, the expected output for each input. Ground truth is optional, and only metrics that compare the agent’s response against a reference use it. To evaluate tool calling, the ground truth must also include the expected tool calls for each test case: which tools the agent should call, in what order, and with what arguments. Everything after that happens inside the UAEF. Figure 1 shows the path a single evaluation takes, from the inputs to the reports and insights. First, an adapter reads the agent’s native execution, its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs, and normalizes it into one canonical trace, so that the steps that follow are identical no matter which framework produced the agent. Next, UAEF screens the trace for personally identifiable information (PII), such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers, before data is stored. The evaluation engine then scores the trace on a selection from 36 built-in metrics across 7 quality dimensions. When you persist a run, UAEF records it as an experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3: Amazon DynamoDB holds the per-experiment metadata used for listing and comparison, and Amazon S3 holds the full results. With runs stored, a team can compare an agent version against a baseline to detect regressions and generate reports and insights that explain what changed and why. Those reports close the loop: the team evaluates the agent, learns what regressed or improved, changes the prompt, model, or tools, and evaluates again. Figure 1: UAEF closed-loop evaluation data flow The rest of this section follows that flow in order: the adapters that make UAEF framework-agnostic, the evaluation engine and its metrics, PII detection, experiment storage and comparison, and the reports that close the loop. Canonical trace and adapters Adapters are what make UAEF framework-agnostic. An adapter reads the record of an agent’s run, including its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs. It converts that record into one canonical representation called the AgentTrace , which is the only thing the rest of UAEF scores. Because of that conversion, UAEF works with the agent, whatever SDK it was built with (such as LangGraph, LangChain, or Strands Agents). It can run locally, behind an HTTP endpoint, or on a managed runtime such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with traces in Langfuse or not captured at all. UAEF provides an adapter for each of these, and they produce the same AgentTrace , so metrics, scores, and comparisons stay consistent across every one of them. A trace reaches UAEF two ways. If one already exists, from a past run, a log, or an observability store, it is handed to UAEF and the matching adapter normalizes it. If not, UAEF invokes the agent for you: given a runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) or an HTTP endpoint, it calls the agent on each dataset input, collects the response, and adapts it in one step. Either way, the output is the same AgentTrace . Because every metric, mode, and report operates on the AgentTrace rather than on a framework native format, the scoring that follows is identical no matter where the trace came from. That separation, normalization first and scoring second, is what lets a team compare an agent built on one framework against an agent built on another on a single scale. Evaluation engine The evaluation engine scores a canonical trace across 7 quality dimensions, each capturing a distinct aspect of agent behavior that a single accuracy number would hide. Tool calling measures whether the agent selected the right tools, called them in a sensible order, and passed valid arguments. Response quality measures whether the final answer is relevant, complete, accurate, and grounded in the provided context rather than hallucinated. Responsible

items.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
items.description: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. items.title: Introducing usage-based pricing for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming
items.description: Usage-based metering for bidirectional streaming solves a software billing problem for real-time speech AI. Customers deploying streaming models on Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming pay for the endpoint infrastructure that hosts the model. Separately, model providers listing on AWS Marketplace need a way to charge for what customers consume during a live stream. Today, we’re announcing usage-based metering for Amazon SageMaker bidirectional (bidi) streaming inference, so model providers can report actual usage for the AWS Marketplace software charge. Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges still apply. Deepgram , the real-time speech AI company, is the launch partner for this capability, bringing usage-based Speech-to-Text (STT) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) billing to AWS Marketplace. This post builds on a series of innovations between Deepgram and AWS. First, we introduced bidirectional streaming for real-time inference on Amazon SageMaker AI , which supports long-lived bidirectional streams between clients and model servers. Then, Deepgram enhanced Amazon SageMaker AI support with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) temporary delegation , simplifying secure authentication for enterprise deployments, and expanded observability with enhanced metrics . Now, with usage-based metering, we further strengthen the foundation for production real-time AI, aligning billing with how customers consume streaming and real-time AI workloads. Why streaming broke the existing billing model With AWS Marketplace software metering for SageMaker AI real-time request-response inference, model providers can report a unit count in an HTTP response header. AWS Marketplace uses that quantity for the software charge. This works for request-response APIs where the billable quantity is known when the response is sent. Bidirectional streaming is different. A client streams audio and receives transcriptions through the SageMaker AI API using an HTTP/2 event stream. SageMaker AI connects to the model server over WebSockets. A session can last 30 seconds or 30 minutes. Usage accumulates as the session runs, and the final total isn’t known until it ends. A response header alone can’t report periodic usage during that live session. Hourly software pricing can charge customers while a model is available, including quiet periods. With usage-based metering, providers can align the AWS Marketplace software charge with reported usage. SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges remain separate and continue to apply while the endpoint is provisioned. How companion metadata streaming works The solution introduces a second WebSocket connection alongside the existing inference stream. When a bidirectional streaming session starts, SageMaker AI establishes two connections to the model server: Data connection : carries inference request and response data, the existing bidirectional stream. Metadata connection : a companion WebSocket dedicated to metering data. Model servers opt in by returning one header on the WebSocket upgrade response: X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Supported: true SageMaker AI then opens a companion WebSocket to the model server at /invocations-bidirectional-stream-metadata . Both connections carry the same X-Amzn-SageMaker-Request-Id header, which the model server uses to correlate metering records with the active inference session. The model server sends metering data as JSON text frames on the metadata connection. Send records at a frequency that matches the billing model: incrementally as usage accrues (recommended), either as each unit is consumed or as periodic batches of units consumed since the previous record. Send any final record as soon as the session ends. Each frame contains exactly one metering record, rather than an array of records. The metadata stream has a rate quota of one message per second per connection, with a maximum message size of 512 bytes. We recommend sending metering records incrementally as usage accrues. This reduces the amount of usage left unreported if a session ends unexpectedly. Transport delivery alone does not establish that usage has been billed. Validate reported units against AWS Marketplace reports and buyer charges. { "Metering": { "Dimension": "inference.count", "ConsumedUnits": 720, "ClientToken": "a3f2b1c0-unique-uuid" } } Metering messages use the inference.count dimension, and ConsumedUnits supplies the quantity for that dimension. If the product charges per second of audio, a record reporting 12 minutes of metered audio carries 720 seconds as ConsumedUnits: 720 . The dimension name doesn’t mean one unit per request. The provider defines which audio counts as metered usage, and the AWS Marketplace offer maps the unit to its price. The listing shows one price per unit, labeled per request, with up to three decimal places. The ClientToken field supports idempotency. If a duplicate token arrives on the same connection, SageMaker AI drops the duplicate message silently. The metadata connection runs over TCP, which provides ordered, reliable delivery at the transport layer. If it fails to establish or drops mid-session, inference continues by default because X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Required defaults to false . Set this header to true when the provider must stop inference if the metadata stream becomes unavailable. This choice trades inference availability for metering continuity. It doesn’t guarantee that malformed or dropped records are billed. What this means for customers If you deploy real-time AI models for transcription, contact centers, voice agents, or captioning, the new metering model changes how the AWS Marketplace software charge is calculated. SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges still apply. Transparent, per-unit billing through AWS Marketplace means usage flows directly into your AWS bill. items.title: Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal
items.description: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app , Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.
