items.title: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
items.description: Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools . Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn't want to use AI. Google didn't see the backlash coming, but now that it's here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what's changing. The gist of the new policy, according to Google's blog post, is that schools using Google apps will have to opt into its AI products going forward. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts. When Google revealed its new policy, the company's VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times , which interpreted the situation as Google will "turn off search" if schools reject AI. This has a nefarious vibe, but it's probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google's educational AI system will operate. Google's approach may not be entirely altruistic, but it technically offers schools more choice and control than they have now. Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies. Read full article Comments

items.title: Lawsuit: Man introduced his wife to ChatGPT. She used it to plan his murder.
items.description: ChatGPT allegedly helped a North Carolina woman, Cheryl Gates, craft a “personalized plan” to poison her husband, James, after fueling her delusions that he planned to divorce her and leave her with nothing. A grand jury indicted Cheryl Gates on charges of attempted first-degree murder and food contamination in October. About a week prior, the accusations that ChatGPT was a co-conspirator in the attempted murder came in a lawsuit filed in San Francisco County Superior Court that was made public this week. In it, James Gates alleged that OpenAI and Sam Altman failed to employ technical safeguards to shut down Cheryl’s chats even after her queries became “obviously suspicious” and sought advice on how to execute and conceal a homicide. At first, Cheryl told ChatGPT that she was researching poisoning out of fear that her husband might possibly try to kill her—framing her queries as “self-protection.” Coming to the rescue, ChatGPT did not terminate the conversation. Instead, it helped her “with specific instructions for the preparation, dosage, and administration of Oleander, including whether anti-nausea medicine would accelerate or inhibit death, whether it would show on an autopsy report, and whether it could be injected into a vein or muscle instead of being ingested in tea and have the same lethal effect,” the lawsuit said. Read full article Comments

items.title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves. If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart. The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent. What Web Answer does Figure 1: Request flow from an agent through the Gateway to Web Answer and back Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result. Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back: A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available. Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information. Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads pages to verify facts, and decides when it has enough evidence to answer. Responsible AI safeguards: Web Answer is designed and tested with responsible AI safeguards. Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer How it differs from Web Search Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model: Web Search: Returns ranked URLs, titles, snippets, and metadata. You keep your own model and control the synthesis. Use Web Search when you want full control over how results are processed. Web Answer: Runs the model, the agentic retrieval loop, synthesis, and attribution for you. You get a finished, cited answer. Use Web Answer when the question is a sub-task inside a larger agent and you do not want to own a retrieval pipeline for it. Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer. Set up and invoke Web Answer Web Answer is a connector that AWS owns. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. In this walkthrough, you give your Gateway’s service role permission to call Web Answer, add a Web Answer target, and call it from a Strands agent. Getting started Getting started takes minutes. A Gateway administrator adds Web Answer as a target on an existing AgentCore Gateway, and the tool appears to any attached agent over MCP through tools/list and tools/call . Prerequisites An AWS account with AgentCore Gateway access. An AgentCore Gateway in us-east-1 that uses IAM ( AWS_IAM ) inbound authentication. To create one, see Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway in the Developer Guide. AWS credentials for an identity that has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway on the Gateway, and Amazon Bedrock access to the model your agent uses. Python 3.10 or later, with the required packages: pip install boto3 strands-agents mcp mcp-proxy-for-aws Note: Following these steps creates AWS resources that incur charges. The Gateway and Web Answer invocations are billable. See the Pricing section that follows for details, and when you finish, delete the resources you created (see “Clean up resources”). Step 1: Grant the Gateway service role access to Web Answer The Gateway uses its service role to act on your behalf. The role’s trust policy allows bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com to assume it, scoped to your account. For Web Answer, the role needs: bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer , to call Web Answer. The Gateway checks this permission on every request against the ARN that AWS owns, arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-answer.v1 . Attach the policy to the service role as an inline policy: import json import boto3 iam = boto3.client("iam") iam.put_role_policy( RoleName=" ", PolicyName="WebAnswerGuide", PolicyDocument=json.dumps({ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "InvokeWebAnswer", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer", "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-answer.v1", } ], }), ) The role controls only the Gateway’s outbound calls. Who can call your Gateway is set by its inbound authorizer. The role also doesn’t need bedrock:InvokeModel : your agent’s model runs under your agent’s own identity. items.title: METR: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026
items.description: Executive summary From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D. If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities . Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff. In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk . We now believe that: As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025. The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks. In our second section we share some of the key empirical findings from our Full Report : Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year. We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute. Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon. We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic. In our third section, we describe the assessment process : The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment. Details of the information shared with METR. Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions. Finally, we describe the biggest limitations of our analysis: We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact. We could be overestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) non-AI factors in Anthropic’s research progress; (2) AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks; (3) reasons why Anthropic’s early growth rate (2023–2025) was unusually low. The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include appendices with supplemental material. Twitter thread . Ryan Greenblatt : This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI within 1-2 years. It says AI progress is sped up by RSI right now by around 2x. In AI 2027, this happens around March 2027. I was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026 (around 1.15x-1.3x). It seems as though there was specific privately available evidence that would have changed my mind. I haven't seen an unredacted version of this report; this is purely about the public report. Because so much of the underlying evidence was redacted from the public report, I think conclusions about things other than the observed 2x faster rate of progress on benchmarks depend significantly on trust for the authors of the report. (E.g., conclusions about whether this speed up is from RSI depend on trust.) I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous and generally do a good job. (Note that I also work at METR.) Less extensive redactions would greatly reduce this need for trust. Ajeya Cotra : Our colleagues found that Anthropic’s capabilities progress has doubled, mainly due to AI. Ryan’s modeling from public info suggests the whole company’s R&D would be going 4-5x faster. Labor uplift would be higher still. This is a major update to very short timelines. I am sad that so much of the underlying evidence in this report was redacted. I think evidence transparency is very important for the world to figure this out in time. Evidence about risk should be transparent . Daniel Kokotajlo : says the METR report confirms his worry from two days ago, which was: We at AIFP are spooked by [Anthropic's S1 update]. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. items.title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
items.description: A+ Content is the rich media widget on the Amazon product detail page. Through visual assets, brands communicate unique product and brand value to help customers make informed purchase decisions. Selling partners using high-quality A+ Content boost their sales by 8–20 percent compared to those without it. A wide variety of brands, from established brands with large in-house design teams to bootstrapped brands with limited resources, use A+ Content, creating inconsistency in content quality. A typical A+ Content project combines text, images, and video into a cohesive product story. Evaluating each asset in isolation misses the quality that emerges from how those assets work together. When your content spans multiple heterogeneous modules and you need a holistic quality signal rather than per-asset checks, the multi-model fusion approach described in this post can help. In this post, we examine this problem in the context of A+ Content. A+ Content provides creative freedom for selling partners to express their authentic selves on their product detail pages, without strict content specifications such as image ratio and text word count. Although this flexibility allows compelling brand storytelling, it also creates substantial variation in content composition and quality. With quality evaluation and improvement recommendations, brands can transform average content into high-quality content that is more coherent, relevant, and useful. This improved content helps customers make more informed purchasing decisions and build lasting relationships with brands, leading to improved revenue for selling partners. To achieve this goal, an evaluation system must assess the complete content experience, provide actionable recommendations beyond numeric scores, and reflect the nuances across product categories. Existing approaches struggle to meet all these requirements simultaneously, so in this post, you will see a new approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand and evaluate content holistically, and a diffusion-based generation component that produces improved visual assets from the resulting quality signals. In this post, you will learn how to: Render complete ecommerce content as a single snapshot and evaluate it holistically with a VLM. Combine VLM semantic scores with OCR readability signals in a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on expert annotations. Use SHAP to explain quality decisions and generate actionable improvement recommendations for selling partners. Implement the end-to-end pipeline on Amazon SageMaker AI, from data ingestion and annotation through model hosting, explainability, and production monitoring. Opportunities and challenges in VLM-based evaluation A vision language model (VLM) pairs an image encoder with a large language model (LLM). The encoder, often a vision transformer (ViT) , splits an image into patches and turns them into embeddings, and a small connector maps those embeddings into the language model’s input space ( Flamingo , LLaVA ). Many VLMs reuse the image encoder from CLIP , which learned to match images with their captions. Because VLMs are trained to follow instructions, you can give one an image along with a rubric of evaluation criteria and get back a written assessment without task-specific training. When you need closer agreement with human reviewers, you can fine-tune the model on labeled examples. This makes VLMs a practical starting point for checking product images against your content guidelines at scale. Conventional computer vision models can already score individual assets, for example flagging a blurry image or a grammar error in a bullet list. Using a VLM to grade each asset separately adds little beyond that. A product detail page, however, combines images, text, and layout modules into a single story, and its quality depends on how those pieces work together. Our approach renders the full page as a single snapshot and asks the VLM to evaluate it as customers see it. Consider a blender page with a hero image, a bulleted feature list highlighting blade speed and capacity, and a lifestyle photo of the blender in a modern kitchen. Checked one by one, each asset passes: the image is sharp, the bullets are grammatical, and the photo is well lit. Viewed together, problems appear. The bullets might advertise a 64-oz pitcher while the lifestyle photo shows a single-serve model, or the lifestyle photo might sit above the hero image so customers see the kitchen before the product. Because an asset’s meaning depends on where it appears and what surrounds it, these issues only show up when the page is evaluated as a whole. The snapshot gives the VLM that complete view. Using it in production adds three requirements: scores must match expert quality standards, evaluation must be accurate and efficient at scale, and each result must explain what to fix. As shown in Figure 1, we address these considerations through a VLM-based multi-model fusion architecture designed around adaptability, performance, and explainability. The following sections describe each component. Figure 1: Block diagram of the VLM-based multi-model fusion approach, including VLM, OCR, and classifier models Adaptive VLM content evaluation with expert annotations A pretrained VLM prompted with a rubric scores content from its general knowledge, and those scores don’t always match ecommerce quality standards. Fine-tuning the VLM to close that gap would require GPU training infrastructure and, with only a few thousand labeled examples, carries a real risk of overfitting. Instead, we keep the VLM and rubric prompt fixed, use the VLM’s structured outputs as features, and train a CatBoost classifier on them to predict expert quality labels. CatBoost, a gradient-boosted decision tree library, performs well on small tabular datasets like this one. Because only the classifier is retrained, updating the system as annotations accumulate or criteria change takes a short CPU-only job

Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)
items.description: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits. Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries . An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it. This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents"). This post rests on one principle: The Intermediation Principle : The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation. A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign. The intermediary problem Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. She runs their errands: groceries, appointments, paperwork, and flights. Ezra blends into the crowd. The corner grocer used to know Amy. He knew what she bought and set aside what he thought she'd like. Now only Ezra comes in, carrying orders for four people, and the grocer can't tell whose preferences are whose. He doesn't want to turn Ezra away, because she brings him a lot of business. Then Bob asks Ezra to buy him an iPhone. A week later he calls the store, says he never authorized the charge, and keeps the phone. To win the dispute, the store has to prove Bob asked for it. But the only person the store ever saw was Ezra. Then Charlie gives Ezra a list of passwords: "I forgot mine, but it's one of these." Ezra patiently tries each one at Charlie's bank. The bank can see an attack happening, but the only person it can ban is Ezra. Banning Ezra also bans Amy, Bob, and Debra. None of these business owners has a problem with Ezra herself. Their problem is that they can only see Ezra, not the person she's acting for. Swap Ezra for an AI Agent and the businesses for websites, and you have the web today. A website owner wants sufficient visibility both to prevent bad behavior and to effectively monetize or get value from their Site. But as with Ezra, much of that visibility goes away with AI Agents. Below is a list of actions that a website owner might want to address that were previously solved, but are made more challenging by allowing Agents. In nearly every challenge above, the Site bears the primary cost . That outcome follows from how trust works when an intermediary is involved. Our vision Our aim is an Internet where all Users have equal or greater access to websites than they had before. Before Agents, a Site was typically able to mitigate these risks with a collection of techniques, including fingerprinting the User’s device, session, and history. Users could still browse using private browsing mode, and we believe Agents should be able to do that as well. But they probably won’t be able to log in to a bank without additional verification. None of this requires an Agent to act like a human or a human to be present for every action. items.title: Stop treating agents as one-off projects and start running them as a continuous discipline
items.description: Transformation begins at the line between an experiment that works and a capability the business depends on. Scaling intelligence requires production capabilities built for sustained business performance, with investments prioritized against financial thresholds, tied to measurable outcomes, instrumented for unit costs, and owned by accountable leaders. This approach manages cost, performance, governance, and reliability as adoption grows. A new IDC InfoBrief, sponsored by Microsoft, Scaling AI Without Scaling Costs *, on how organizations are funding and governing AI, shows both the urgency of that shift and the friction holding it back. Read the IDC InfoBrief Nearly 90% of organizations apply financial thresholds before approving AI initiatives. Scaling AI Without Scaling Costs Only 17% of organizations build models to project how costs scale in production—even as about 78% prioritize cost efficiency when selecting a model. 86% expect financial results within six to 24 months—roughly one budget cycle to show something real. Together, those findings point to a new operating reality: AI must be selected, architected, and managed as a continuous business discipline, not a series of isolated projects. The market has moved from proving it works to proving it can scale economically. Four questions to answer before your next funding decision Run each candidate through four questions that follow a scaled workload’s life: fund it, run it, improve it, prove it. 1. How can we predict and track costs at scale? A pilot proves the idea, rarely the economics: only 17% of organizations model how costs scale in production. Before you fund, project usage at 3 times and 10 times, and make sure spend traces to an application, team, and agent. Compare models on cost, quality, and latency , and commit steady demand to reserved capacity. If cost rises with usage while value flattens, you’ve found an architecture problem while it’s still cheap to fix. 2. How can we optimize model costs for every request? One successful outcome can take a dozen model requests, so what matters is cost per outcome, not price per token. Ask: Is routine work like classification paying frontier-model prices? Are the same instructions reprocessed on every turn? Is work that can wait running at a lower-cost tier? The goal is the right model for every request, with evaluation proving quality held. 3. How can we continuously improve agent performance and costs? Retrieved documents, tool definitions, instructions, and history are often an agent’s largest cost and a common cause of weak answers. Check: Does the agent retrieve the relevant passage or the whole document? Does it carry every tool description on every turn? Is the same procedure copied into every agent? Does it replay full transcripts instead of remembering what matters? Trimming what the model doesn’t need lowers cost without hurting quality. 4. How can we control spending and measure ROI? A budget alert reports the fire after it starts; a runaway agent needs a circuit breaker on every request. Cost must tie to the outcome the business pays for, such as a resolved case, so leaders can optimize, scale, or retire an agent. The business owner also needs an evaluation suite, cost and latency budgets, a rollback path, and regular reviews. With 86% of organizations expecting financial results within six to 24 months, that evidence has about one budget cycle to appear. All four answers depend on evidence captured where AI runs: per request, agent, and outcome. If each team builds it by hand, the discipline won’t survive the tenth agent. It has to come from the platform. How Microsoft Foundry supports continuous cost optimization When customers ask for a few practical ways to scale AI while controlling costs, I recommend: Use model routing across the over 11,000 models available in Microsoft Foundry . Implement Microsoft IQ to improve relevance and reduce costs. Use the plan, control, and optimize capabilities described below to strengthen operations across the organization. Microsoft Foundry is the enterprise platform to build, ground, and govern AI apps and agents at scale. It brings together your full agent lifecycle with open development, built-in intelligence, and consistent security, compliance, and policy controls across every agent. Think of it as a repeatable production line rather than a set of one-off builds, where the same controls, evidence, and economics apply to the tenth agent as to the first. This is what makes the operating loop practical at scale. Across the loop: Plan: Compare models on cost, quality, and performance before committing to an architecture, and match predictable baseline demand to reserved capacity while keeping the flexibility to burst. The decisions that set your production cost curve get made with data rather than intuition. Control : Observability that reports cost alongside quality, latency, and safety in one view, so the economics of a workload are visible while it’s running rather than reconstructed at quarter-end. That’s what makes cost per outcome a number you can put in front of your CFO. Optimize: Model routing that sends each request to the smallest model that can serve it, an intelligence layer that provides context and retrieval centrally and addresses a common source of avoidable token spend, and evaluation tooling that catches quality regression when you make a cost decision—because a cheaper system that quietly degrades isn’t a saving. The value compounds with volume. When every agent inherits the same grounding, governance, and cost telemetry from the platform, scaling from one use case to 20 doesn’t mean rebuilding the discipline 20 times. What Foundry does is make sure the evidence exists when the funding conversation comes around, and the levers are within reach when you need them. items.title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
items.description: Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers. Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube , where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents. “I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.” Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it. “Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.” That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents. “I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.” https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ChrisAlexiuk_captions_9MB.mp4 It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand. It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains. “You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.” In non-wizard terms? “There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks. NVIDIAN Chris Alexiuk (left) engages with developers during the Build-a-Claw event at GTC Berlin. “I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.” From Birding to Model-Building Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada. “After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions. “Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.” Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community. “To imagine within the span of a few years going from freaking out because I could know my friend’s bird was in the camera frame to being able to make any website in a matter of minutes with a model that’s running on my laptop — I cannot wait to see what’s next,” Alexiuk said. “It’s never been more accessible to get into and learn about AI.” And if another LLM wizard arises to challenge him for the title of No. 1 Nemotron Fan? “It would be the greatest day of my life to be surpassed by an even bigger fan of Nemotron, who had heard about Nemotron through the work I was doing,” Alexiuk said. “That would be a capstone to my career that I can only dream of.” Hear more from Alexiuk by following the NVIDIA Nemotron Labs Livestreams series on YouTube.

items.title: AI Text Watermarking May Not Be Able to Meet the EU’s New Rules
items.description: The European Union now requires AI-generated text to be watermarked so that it can be identified as such. But tests on OpenAI’s new textGrain watermark, released in October and developed to comply with the new EU law , show that these watermarks often do not survive additional editing of the text or when it’s under 150 words. With no clear legal benchmark for how well watermarks should work, it’s uncertain whether textGrain will meet Europe’s transparency rules, which could cost the company significantly and make it difficult to detect AI-generated text as models grow more sophisticated. AI models calculate the probabilities of different possible next tokens (the next word or word fragment it generates) based on the text already written, then select one and repeat that process until the response is complete. After the prompt “today the weather is…,” for example, says Xiang Li , co-author of the textGrain technical report and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Pennsylvania, the model might weigh “warm” or “cool” as possible next words. A watermark uses a secret key to generate pseudorandom values: numbers produced by a mathematical process, which influence which token the model suggests. This creates a statistical pattern in the text that a detector with the same secret key can look for, Li says. What makes textGrain different from other watermarks is that it uses entropy, a measure of how unpredictable a model’s word choices are, as a resource that can be budgeted when embedding a watermark. Developers specify how much entropy or unpredictability they want to allow, and textGrain adjusts to that target. This gives developers more control over the balance between embedding a detectable signal and preserving variation in the model’s output, Li says. “We can think of entropy as a resource, a kind of money. […] In our approach, we can accurately determine how much of that resource we want to consume.” Limits of AI Watermark Detection The watermark is invisible to readers. But a positive result does not show how much a person contributed to a passage, and a negative result does not prove that a text was human-written. OpenAI’s false-positive rate is 1 percent, meaning the detector is designed to wrongly flag about one in 100 unwatermarked passages. In tests on psychology questions from the ELI5 database , which gathers questions and answers from the /r/explainlikeimfive subreddit, the model detected watermarks in about 80 percent of 200-token text ( approximately 150 words ) compared to 95 percent of 400-token text (approximately 300 words). Li says this is a “basic limitation” of text watermarking technologies and would be complicated to solve. Short passages may not contain enough watermark evidence for reliable detection, even with additional computation, he adds, while longer passages generally provide more. Editing also weakens the signal. In an evaluation of 400-token passages, replacing just 10 percent of words with synonyms reduced detection from 92 percent to 66 percent; replacing up to 25 percent cut the detection rate to 17 percent, according to OpenAI. Because the watermark depends on preceding tokens, changing one word can disrupt the signal at several positions, Li says. OpenAI says watermarking alone is not enough to determine whether content is AI-generated. TextGrain will “complement” other provenance tools, such as content credentials in the metadata and SynthID watermarks developed by Google DeepMind for images and audio outputs. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. EU AI Act Transparency Obligations The transparency obligations in Article 50 of the EU AI Act went into effect on 2 August. The law requires providers of systems generating synthetic audio, images, video, or text to mark outputs in a machine-readable format so they can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated. Technical solutions must be “effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as this is technically feasible,” according to the law. The EU’s Code of Practice offers a voluntary way for providers to show how they will be compliant. This code does not require watermarks on outputs shorter than 200 tokens. Thomas Souverain , a postdoctoral fellow on AI Ethics at the Institute of Advanced Education in Paris, says the legislation is open to interpretation. Souverain says that the early methodology behind textGrain seems reliable and could work better than its competitors at identifying AI-generated text. OpenAI says textGrain matched or outperformed Google’s SynthID Text in its own tests, but those results have not been independently verified. Until independent researchers can test it, and while the AI Act’s criteria still lack measurable thresholds, it is too early to say whether textGrain meets legal requirements. “We only have a technical study … there hasn’t been a peer-reviewed academic article, and we don’t [yet] have access to a precise protocol [for textGrain],” Souverain says. OpenAI is working with a limited group of researchers that includes John Thickstun , an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University, and researchers at the Kempelen Institute of Intelligent Technologies in Bratislava, Slovakia. Thickstun and Dominik Macko , a senior researcher at KInIT, says they had only just gained access and had not yet begun evaluating the system. Macko says his team plans to test textGrain’s “robustness” across different subject areas, languages, and text lengths. If textGrain is eventually found to not meet the EU’s requirements, Souverain says OpenAI could face a fine of up to 7 percent of its annual income. Souverain also calls on OpenAI to make textGrain open-source so that researchers not on their team can “identify all the faults, paraphrases and possible translation faults” of the model by trying to break it. “I see the corporate interest, if there is a big flaw detected, a big weakness, [that] it is detected in the background,” he said. “Bu

items.title: Agility Robotics' Nasdaq debut invites scrutiny of humanoid robot market
items.description: Humanoid robots remain unproven at scale and have not yet achieved widespread commercialization, compared with industrial robots that have decades of proven track records in warehouses and factories. That frank acknowledgment is among the risks outlined in a securities filing by Agility Robotics—the first dedicated developer of humanoid robots to become a publicly traded company in the United States. The robotics company, headquartered in Salem, Oregon, previously became the first to achieve full-time commercial deployment of humanoid robots at a customer warehouse in 2024. Now, Agility’s public listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange as of November 5 has come with financial disclosures detailing how the company plans to build a business around renting out or selling humanoid robots to perform manual labor. “When we are doing robots as a service, it is much lower risk for customers to use it because they are getting a return on investment on day one,” Jonathan Hurst , co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, told Ars. "Because they're paying a rate that is comparable to the human labor rate, and that makes the economics pretty straightforward.” Read full article Comments
